primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase II catalyzes rapid interconversion of carbon dioxide and water with carbonic acid/bicarbonate and protons. Loss of CA2 impairs osteoclast generation of protons needed for bone resorption and disrupts renal acid-base handling, producing osteopetrosis together with renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy has short stature, recurrent fractures, and delayed dentition. Radiographs show diffuse osteosclerosis. Laboratory studies demonstrate a chronic normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and head CT shows intracranial calcifications. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in CA2.
lead: Which of the following cellular abnormalities most directly explains this child's increased bone density?
correct: Impaired generation of protons by osteoclasts, reducing acidification of the resorption lacuna and mineral dissolution
distractors: Failure of cathepsin K to degrade collagen after normal acidification of the resorption lacuna
Failure of RANK signaling resulting in markedly reduced osteoclast differentiation
Accumulation of extracellular pyrophosphate due to deficient tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase
Defective type I collagen synthesis by osteoblasts
distractor_notes: CTSK loss causes pycnodysostosis and defective organic matrix proteolysis; CA2 deficiency chiefly impairs proton generation and acidification.
RANK pathway defects can cause osteoclast-poor osteopetrosis but do not explain the characteristic renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification of CA2 deficiency.
ALPL deficiency causes hypophosphatasia with impaired mineralization rather than osteopetrosis.
Type I collagen defects produce osteogenesis imperfecta rather than the CA2-associated osteopetrosis/RTA syndrome.
key_expl: Carbonic anhydrase II is required for efficient intracellular proton generation. In osteoclasts, those protons are secreted into the resorption lacuna to acidify the bone surface and dissolve mineral. CA2 deficiency therefore impairs bone resorption, causing osteopetrosis. Carbonic anhydrase II is also important in renal acid-base transport, explaining the associated renal tubular acidosis; cerebral calcification is another characteristic feature.
objective: Explain osteopetrosis in carbonic anhydrase II deficiency as impaired osteoclast proton generation and resorption-lacuna acidification.
